doc.title: Tommy Newsom and Ross Tompkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Studio work in New York and changes
summary: Tommy's early New York studio work came by referrals, and the studio environment was once less electronic.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: What’s it like today doing, you’re still doing studio work and has that changed over the years with how studios have changed and electronics and all that. Has that affected your business?

Oh, Lord, in the greatest way. When I started doing some studio work in New York the first year I was there, I got more work from fallout, I mean from referrals, because they would get through all the busy guys. I got more work then the last year I was in New York. Either that or they had all heard me and there was no more calls. But I prefer to think of the other.
Well what I’m trying to say is see at that time there was no, hardly no, the electronic things were like guitars and a Leslie organ or something. But they would have five saxes.

You could get your feet wet, you know you could get used to being in the studio with the red light on because if you started, if you’d go there like as the only sax, I’ve had that happen too. It’s a terrible feeling if you’re not used to it. Because all your perceptions change. If you — I got that kind of mind where things bother me.
